newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China leaders to face HK protests over Tiananmen.
newsitem.headline: China leaders to face HK protests over Tiananmen.

text.p: Chinese leaders attending Hong Kong's handover to China at the end of the month can expect to face pro-democracy protests in the territory over Beijing's bloody crackdown on the 1989 Tiananmen Square demonstrations.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng will also face calls for the release of all Chinese dissidents, the end of one-party rule, and the establishment of a democratic China, the South China Morning Post said on Sunday.
Jiang and Li are to lead the Chinese delegation at the ceremonies marking China's recovery of Hong Kong from Britain at midnight on June 30, after 156 years of colonial rule.
The protests will be staged by the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of the Patriotic Democratic Movement in China, a democracy lobby branded by China as subversive.

The alliance was spawned by the 1989 student-led pro-democracy protests in Beijing, which ended in a bloody military crackdown with heavy loss of life. Li is widely seen to have played a key role in the crackdown.

Future Secretary of Justice Elsie Leung has warned pro-democracy activists not to defy post-handover laws governing protests in the few hours between the handover and the passage of a bill putting them into effect in the early morning of July 1, the Hong Kong Standard newspaper said.

Leung said there would be no legal vacuum as the bills would be made retroactive to midnight on June 30, and she would also exercise her discretion in prosecuting any unlawful deomonstration held shortly after the change of rule.
If anyone tried to make use of those few hours to act against the laws, she would use her discretion in deciding whether or not to prosecute them, Leung told the Standard.
The laws to be confirmed include a provision requiring organisers of demonstrations to obtain a permit.
Apart from the Alliance, the popular Democratic Party is also planning a democracy protest shortly after the handover.
Party chairman Martin Lee urged Hong Kong people on Sunday to stand up for their freedoms and rights, with just nine days to go before the handover.
Speaking on the radio, he urged them to take the assurances given by Beijing and future leader Tung chee-hwa on maintaining the territory's freedoms at face value.
"Chinese leaders and Mr Tung say freedoms will continue unabridged, but will they? That depends entirely on the people of Hong Kong and not on the Chinese leaders," he said.
He called on people not to exercise self-censorship to please Beijing. "If we voluntarily give up some of our rights and freedoms, we have no one but ourselves to blame."
A poll by the South China Morning Post released on Sunday found that support for Hong Kong's democracy camp was rising in the run-up to the handover.

Some 43.8 percent of those who answered backed the Democratic Party, up from 39.5 percent last month, it said. Adding the supporters of three smaller parties, the democratic camp had the support of 68.7 percent of those answering.
